title: Building a trading bot that may eventually graduate to live trading—looking for criticism of my validation process
author: Colombian_Ronin
selftext:
I’m building a private Python trading system and would appreciate feedback from people with experience developing and validating automated strategies.

The system currently operates in research, backtesting, paper-trading, and shadow modes. It cannot place live orders yet. The eventual goal is to graduate a genuinely validated strategy to small-scale live trading with strict risk controls.

I’m intentionally keeping live execution disabled until a strategy produces enough evidence to justify taking that step. I’m not selling anything, and I’m not claiming the system is profitable.

My primary concern is avoiding overfitting and false confidence from attractive backtests.

The system currently:

* Processes one-minute historical candle data.
* Tests strategies candle by candle.
* Estimates commissions, bid/ask spread, and slippage.
* Divides data chronologically into training and unseen testing samples.
* Selects parameters using only the training sample.
* Locks the selected parameters before evaluating unseen data.
* Divides unseen data into four chronological walk-forward periods.
* Measures performance in quiet and volatile regimes.
* Tests nearby parameter combinations for stability.
* Runs a 2,000-path circular block-bootstrap Monte Carlo analysis.
* Tracks net R, drawdown, win rate, trade count, execution costs, and results without the best trade.
* Separates bullish and bearish performance.
* Rejects strategies that fail minimum sample size, unseen profitability, walk-forward consistency, regime, or robustness requirements.
* Supports several separate strategy families.
* Keeps secondary strategy results from overriding the qualification rules for the primary strategy.
* Can eventually run approved strategies in real-time shadow and paper modes before any live capital is considered.

My current qualification requirements include:

* At least 20 training trades.
* At least 20 unseen trades.
* Positive performance after estimated costs.
* At least three of four positive walk-forward periods.
* Positive results in every materially represented market regime.
* At least 60% of nearby parameter combinations remaining acceptable.
* No changes to the locked strategy after viewing unseen results.

No strategy has passed every requirement yet.

One recent TSLA result produced:

* 10 training trades.
* 9 unseen trades.
* Approximately +10.4R on unseen data.
* Three of four positive walk-forward periods.
* A 77.8% unseen win rate.
* 100% profitable paths in that particular 2,000-path Monte Carlo run.
* Approximately 17% nearby-parameter robustness.

The system rejected it because the sample was too small and the nearby settings were unstable. Although the headline result looks promising, I don’t consider nine unseen trades sufficient evidence.

A BA candidate produced approximately +4.35R with around 93% profitable Monte Carlo paths, but it also failed other validation requirements.

My proposed next feature is a candidate incubator. When a result looks promising but lacks evidence, the system would:

* Freeze its exact rules and parameters.
* Record a fingerprint of the strategy.
* Accumulate genuinely new market data.
* Prevent further parameter adjustment.
* Track progress toward minimum sample requirements.
* Compare real-time shadow fills with simulated fills.
* Retire the candidate if performance deteriorates.
* Prevent live graduation until every requirement is satisfied.

The tentative graduation process is:

1. Historical training and unseen-data testing.
2. Walk-forward, regime, cost, robustness, and Monte Carlo validation.
3. A final untouched holdout dataset.
4. Several weeks or months of real-time shadow signals.
5. Paper execution with realistic fill assumptions.
6. Manual approval for initial live trades.
7. Very small position sizes using money I can afford to lose.
8. Hard limits on position size, daily loss, consecutive losses, and total drawdown.
9. An emergency stop that disables new orders.
10. Gradual scaling only if live execution resembles validated results.

I’d appreciate criticism of the methodology, particularly:

* Are these qualification gates sensible?
* Is 20 training and 20 unseen trades still far too small?
* How would you construct and protect a final untouched dataset?
* Is circular block bootstrapping appropriate for a sequence of trades?
* How should block size be selected?
* How should parameter stability be measured?
* Which execution costs or failure conditions am I overlooking?
* How long should shadow and paper testing run before risking live capital?
* What would you require before allowing even manually approved live orders?
* Which tests have been most effective at exposing strategies that were overfit?

My objective is not to make a backtest look impressive. I’m trying to develop a process that makes it difficult for an unreliable strategy to reach live trading.

comments.author: teckel
comments.body:
What's interesting is that just 20 minutes after your post, I finished up a similar post on my autonomous AI-powered trading agent: [https://www.reddit.com/r/ai\_trading/s/AtMbwtQhV5](https://www.reddit.com/r/ai_trading/s/AtMbwtQhV5)

What's interesting to me is that we're going about it in a VERY different way, they're about as far apart as they could be.  Mine is more of swing trading agent (so looking for 2 week to 2 month holding periods), and using common strategies instead of finding new strategies.

Anyway, mine is live and making trades with real money (I've been slowly feeding it more money daily), so I've got a whopping $725 on the line at this point.

What are your goals for holding periods?  Trading stocks or options?  And a big one, how and when do you exit a position?

replies.author: Colombian_Ronin
replies.body:
Mine currently targets intraday trades rather than multi-week swing trades. It processes one-minute closed candles, allows up to about 20 minutes for an entry, and limits a position to roughly 60 minutes. I’m avoiding overnight exposure for now.

The initial focus is liquid stocks and ETFs. Options are a separate research track because spreads, implied volatility, liquidity, assignment risk, and Greeks make realistic testing more complicated.

Exits are defined before entry: a structural stop-loss, a reward-to-risk profit target, and a time-based exit if neither is reached within the maximum holding period. I’m trying to keep those rules deterministic instead of letting an AI invent a new exit explanation while a trade is losing.

The long-term goal is real-money trading, but it’s still in paper/shadow validation. If it passes untouched forward testing, I’d start with very small capital and strict loss limits before increasing it.

For your live agent, does the AI independently decide when to exit, or are its exits constrained by fixed risk rules? How are you measuring drawdown, slippage, and performance against a basic benchmark?

replies.author: teckel
replies.body: AI helps identify and score by looking at big data. There's always a deterministic process after the AI does it's thing. The deterministic side has hard gates and can override anything the AI suggests. The exits and trims are almost 100% pre-defined and deterministic. I also use several sets of exit rules based on the strategy used to find and decided to buy the stock. For example, a pivot has a different exit strategy than a momentum or mean-reversion strategy.

comments.author: IGOSODAMNHAM
comments.body:
* Processes one-minute historical candle data.

If you use any lagging indicators such as moving averages, make sure you are not getting the sma data before the candle is closed or use smaller timeframes for entries. For example an SMA 200 on a daily candle will move large amounts throughout the day and using the result to trade on that day is cheating.

replies.author: Colombian_Ronin
replies.body: Good point. Signals are currently calculated at the close of a one-minute candle, and simulated fills begin on the following candle, so the backtest does not use the completed signal bar to enter earlier on that same bar. I still need to add an explicit safeguard for live data that excludes the currently forming candle, because some APIs return an unfinished latest bar. I’ll also add a regression test confirming that modifying the live candle cannot change already-issued signals.
